title: Classical Literature and the Science of Reading: When Two Worlds Collide
author: Jennifer Ramirez
summary: Jennifer Ramirez argues that the Science of Reading (as synthesized in Doug Lemov's new book) and classical education's commitment to reading whole great books are complementary, not competing, approaches. She lays out Lemov's seven research-based pillars of reading instruction and argues classical educators must sustain rigorous, explicit reading instruction well beyond the early phonics years so students can fully access the 'Great Conversation.'
points: Ramirez frames the essay around reconciling the Science of Reading with classical education's commitment to whole, unabridged great books.
She argues reading whole books (not excerpts) builds cognitive stamina and honors the integrity of an author's work.
Citing Descartes, C.S. Lewis, and Robert Hutchins, she argues great books train students' moral imagination and virtue through shared, communal reading and conversation.

She summarizes Lemov, Driggs, and Woolway's seven arguments for reading instruction: managing attention, fluency, background knowledge, vocabulary as knowledge, writing to build reading power, reading whole books, and close reading.
She warns of a major gap: most phonics instruction ends by third grade, leaving many years of schooling without explicit reading instruction if whole-book teaching is abandoned.
She calls on classical educators to sustain the same intensity of reading instruction well beyond elementary years so students reach canonical authors like Shakespeare and Plato.
quotes: In the fifteen years since I cracked open the pages of the first edition of Teach Like a Champion, I’ve appreciated the translation of research that Doug and his team provide to educators around the world.
At the most foundational level, reading creates cognitive stamina. In the age of “snack-size” (and often digital) content, reading whole books
The value of immersing students in great texts, as Descartes described, is “like a conversation with the finest men of past centuries.
As Robert Hutchins, the fifth president of the University of Chicago, proclaimed, “all should be actively and continuously engaged in the Great Conversation” as it is the “road to education.
Reading has the power to unlock worlds, but unlike oral language, it cannot be acquired through exposure or imitation.
Background Knowledge as Comprehension: Comprehension is not a “transferable skill” but a result of background knowledge. To understand a text, students must have a deep, extensive knowledge base.

If most phonics instruction ends around third grade, this leaves at least nine years of schooling potentially without foundational, purposeful, and explicit reading instruction, if we abandon the teaching of whole books.
As educators, may we measure our success, at least in one way, by how deeply and actively students engage in the Great Conversation long after they leave the chairs within our classroom walls.
